name: Omar Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a live-line crew, which means we work on lines while the power's still on, so hospitals and factories don't have to shut down for us. Last year the company bought a robotic arm that sits on the end of the boom, and they picked my crew to run the trial, so half my days now I'm working it with a remote control from inside the bucket. The other half it's the old way, rubber gloves up to the shoulder and very slow, careful hands. Before work I use an AI assistant to plan the day, check the weather and draft my job reports, every day, it's just part of how I work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted with the hard jobs, and I like the arm, it's like a new tool that's half a colleague. What wears me out is the waiting, permits and outage windows that get moved three times. I still live with my parents, I pay them rent and I'm putting the rest away, because one day I want to start a line contracting firm with my older brother Karim, who already runs a small digging business. Friday prayers, Sunday football, and a lot of evenings with spreadsheets of what the trucks would cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it didn't live up to the hype, but the useful bits are still useful. At work I'd keep using it for planning and reports, and I'd keep pushing for the robot arm because that's working. I might post something on a lineworkers' forum about which tools are actually worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for my plans. The contracting firm was always going to be built on good people and good trucks, not on AI. I'd just keep saving and start it when the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, I've got about five months of money now, and I want enough to put in my half for a second-hand bucket truck. Karim and I would probably start doing small private jobs on weekends, like new connections for farm buildings, to build a name. Then in two or three years, if it's going well, I'd leave the company and go full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Focused, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start with weekend jobs. Wouldn't your employer mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As long as it's not their customers and I'm not on call, it's allowed, I've checked the contract. And honestly the company is short of contractors, so in a few years they might be my biggest customer. That's the plan, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Karim think of the robot arm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks I'm mad for it, he's a shovel-and-digger man. But he's also the one who taught me to look at the numbers. When I showed him the arm does a crossarm change with two people instead of four, he went very quiet and asked how much it costs.

S0.say: I'd say it didn't live up to the hype but the useful bits are still useful, and keep using it for planning and pushing for the robot arm. I might post on a lineworkers' forum about which tools are worth paying for.
S0.think: It changes nothing for my plans, because the contracting firm was always going to be built on good people and good trucks, not on AI. I'd keep saving and start it when the numbers work.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving from about five months of cover towards his half of a second-hand bucket truck. Starts weekend private jobs with Karim to build a name, planning to leave the company and go full-time within two or three years.
S0.quote: When I showed him the arm does a crossarm change with two people instead of four, he went very quiet and asked how much it costs.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is entrepreneurial, disciplined and already running a robotic arm trial. Living with his parents to save is both traditional and strategic. His business plans with his brother don't depend on AI at all, so the plateau barely registers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get in early, not complain. At work I'd tell the lads the robots are coming either way, so be the one holding the remote. I'd probably write about it on the forum, the real experience, not the sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the best picture for me. Companies would need contractors who know how to run robots on live lines, and I'd be one of the few who's actually done it. That's exactly the gap Karim and I could fill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the plan. In the first year I'd get Karim and me registered as a business, buy the second-hand truck, and lease a robotic arm if a supplier will do it. I'd use AI for the bids and the scheduling from day one, and I'd stay at the company part-time for the first year if they'll let me, so we have a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lease the arm. How much would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know exactly, the company won't tell me what they paid. I've heard about the price of a small house, which is why leasing makes more sense. If I can't lease one, we start without it and buy later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work who'd be hurt by this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older lads on the glove crew, maybe. Hamid's been doing live work for twenty-five years, he's the best I've seen with his hands. I'd offer him a job, honestly, because a firm needs someone like that to teach the robot operators what good work looks like.

S1.say: I'd say this is the time to get in early, not complain, and tell the lads the robots are coming so be the one holding the remote. I'd write about the real experience on the forum, not the sales pitch.
S1.think: This is the best picture for me, because companies would need contractors who can run robots on live lines and I'm one of the few who's done it. That's exactly the gap Karim and I could fill.
S1.do: Registers a business with Karim in the first year, buys a second-hand truck and tries to lease a robotic arm. Uses AI for bids and scheduling from day one and stays part-time at the company for the first year as a safety net.
S1.quote: I'd tell the lads the robots are coming either way, so be the one holding the remote.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as exactly the opening his firm needs. He's willing to take risk but keeps a part-time safety net, which is prudent. He'd hire his older colleague rather than leave him behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, and the people who move quickly will do better than the ones waiting for the government to save them. At work I'd tell everyone to learn the robots now. Online I'd probably say the same, though some people would hate me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years worries me more than I'd say. If robots can do the whole job by 2028, then the big companies just buy fleets of them and don't need a small firm like ours. My plan is built on there being a gap for a few years, and two years might close it before we've paid off the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the firm, but smaller and faster, no truck loan, just my savings and Karim's digger, doing jobs with the robot arm on a lease. I'd keep my company job as long as I could while doing contract weekends. And I'd keep the savings in cash rather than tying it all up in trucks, because I'd need to move fast if it went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd still feel like I had a plan, but the clock would be loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should move rather than wait for the government. What if moving doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have my family, my savings, and my brother. My parents came here with less than that and built a life. I'd rather fail trying than sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would tell me not to risk my savings, and my dad would tell me to do it but not to borrow. That's always their split. I'd probably listen to my dad, but I'd keep enough aside to calm my mum down.

S2.say: I'd say it's coming and people who move quickly will do better than those waiting for the government. At work and online I'd tell everyone to learn the robots now, though some would hate me for it.
S2.think: Two years worries me more than I'd say. If robots can do the whole job by 2028, big companies buy fleets and don't need a small firm like ours, and the gap my plan depends on might close before we've paid off the truck.
S2.do: Starts the firm smaller and faster with his savings, Karim's digger and a leased robot arm, avoiding a truck loan. Keeps his company job alongside weekend contracts and holds savings in cash to move fast.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with a plan still in hand but a loud clock.
S2.quote: My parents came here with less than that and built a life. I'd rather fail trying than sit and wait.
S2.fieldNote: His free-market instinct is to move first, but he privately sees that big companies could make a small firm pointless in two years. He adjusts by cutting debt rather than ambition. His fallback is family, not the state, which he frames through his parents' story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance, if you're willing to work for it. At work I'd tell the younger lads to get trained on the robots now. I'd probably say the government should get out of the way and let people set up firms quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is about perfect for me. It's enough to build the firm, get a reputation and pay off a truck before the big companies catch up. After that, I'd have to see, but I'd be thirty-two with a business to sell or change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year Karim and I would register the business and buy the second-hand truck with a small loan, and lease the robot arm. I'd leave the company by year two once we had enough contracts. I'd put most of the profit back into the business and keep six months of savings aside for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should get out of the way. What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Permits, mostly. It took the company eight months to get the arm approved for live work, and a small firm can't wait eight months. If the rules said, here's how to get a robot approved in six weeks, small firms would have a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the firm in 2031, when it all arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe we sell it to a bigger company that wants our contracts and our people. Maybe we become the firm that maintains the robots in our region. I'd rather have something to sell than nothing.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a real chance if you're willing to work for it, and tell the younger lads to train on the robots now. I'd say the government should get out of the way and let people set up firms quickly.
S3.think: Five years is about perfect for me: enough to build the firm, get a reputation and pay off a truck before big companies catch up. After that I'd be thirty-two with a business to sell or change.
S3.do: Registers the business with Karim in year one, buys a second-hand truck with a small loan and leases a robot arm. Leaves the company by year two once contracts allow, reinvests most profit and keeps six months of personal savings.
S3.feel: Calm and busy rather than worried.
S3.quote: If the rules said, here's how to get a robot approved in six weeks, small firms would have a chance.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits his business plan almost exactly, so he's calmer here than with two. His one political ask is faster approvals, not support. He's honest that he doesn't know what happens to the firm when AGI fully arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. That sounds harsh, but it's what I think. At work I'd be encouraging everyone to learn the robots and maybe start something on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is great for me. It's enough time to build a proper firm with several trucks and maybe a dozen people, and to be one of the companies that owns robots instead of being replaced by them. At thirty-seven, I could be running a decent business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the same plan as the five-year one but bigger: register the business, buy the truck, lease the arm, and leave the company within two years. Around year four or five I'd buy our own robots and train our people to run them. I'd keep some savings outside the business, because my dad would never forgive me otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. Would you say that to Hamid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not to his face, and he's not the kind who wouldn't prepare, he just has fewer years left. Fair point. I'd still give him a job, and I'd say he's an exception, but maybe there are more exceptions than I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 2036 look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A yard with our name on the gate, four or five trucks, robots on the booms and people in the buckets checking them. Karim running the digging side, me running the line side. Maybe married by then, my mum would want that more than the business.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame, which sounds harsh but is what I think. At work I'd encourage everyone to learn the robots and start something on the side.
S4.think: Ten years is great for me: enough to build a proper firm with several trucks and a dozen people, and be a company that owns robots instead of being replaced by them. At thirty-seven I could be running a decent business.
S4.do: Registers the business, buys the truck, leases the arm and leaves the company within two years. Buys the firm's own robots around year four or five and trains staff to run them, while keeping savings outside the business.
S4.quote: A yard with our name on the gate, four or five trucks, robots on the booms and people in the buckets checking them.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he aims to become an owner of robots rather than a worker replaced by them. His harsh line on personal responsibility softens when an older colleague is named, and he concedes the point gracefully. Family remains his anchor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it might close the gap before a small firm like ours can get going, and then it's only the big companies with robots. What would help is fast, simple rules for small firms to get robots approved, and maybe cheap loans for tradespeople starting businesses, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. If it's only the big companies, people like me end up working for them or not working. If small firms can own a few, then trades people get a piece of it.

headlineQuote: I like the arm, it's like a new tool that's half a colleague.
portrait: Omar Usman is a 27-year-old live-line crew lead whose crew runs the company's trial of a robotic arm on a bucket truck. He lives with his parents, pays them rent and has about five months saved towards a line contracting firm with his older brother Karim. He uses AI every day and believes in moving first rather than waiting for government. He's calm through the plateau, steady change and the slower AGI pictures, which he sees as openings for the firm, but AGI in two years makes him uneasy because big companies could buy robot fleets before a small firm gets going.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it could close the gap for small firms before his gets going, leaving only big companies with robots.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, simple rules for small firms to get robots approved, and cheap loans for tradespeople starting businesses rather than handouts.
